query: For high-entropy alloys intended for demanding engineering applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs the retention or loss of toughness, and why? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, the predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys, the retention of toughness under demanding service conditions is governed by the morphology of the grain boundaries; specifically, inducing a serrated grain boundary topology via controlled, slower cooling after solution treatment enhances toughness by redistributing local strains and delaying crack initiation.
generation.material_initial_state: A precipitation-strengthened high-entropy alloy (for example, one produced by selective laser melting with a baseline straight grain boundary morphology, as in PMC9848264).
generation.intervention: Implement a controlled, slower cooling rate post-solution treatment to induce grain boundary serration, compared to a standard fast cooling that produces straight boundaries.
generation.conditions: Testing performed under high-temperature tensile and creep conditions (e.g., around 650°C) where ductility loss is typically observed.
generation.structural_mediator: The grain boundary morphology, with serrated boundaries facilitating more even strain distribution and promoting in situ formation of damage-mitigating features (e.g., amorphous nanobridges at crack tips).
generation.mechanism: Serrated grain boundaries redistribute and lower local stress concentrations during deformation, thereby delaying grain boundary decohesion and crack initiation. This modification permits the accumulation of energy-dissipating microstructural changes (such as amorphization or nanobridge formation) near crack tips, effectively retaining toughness relative to the baseline with straight grain boundaries.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys processed with slower cooling that yield serrated grain boundaries will exhibit significantly higher tensile fracture strains and improved creep rupture life (potentially increased by factors similar to those observed in PMC9848264) relative to baseline alloys with straight boundaries.
generation.baseline: Identical alloy processed under standard (faster) cooling conditions that results in predominantly straight grain boundaries, known to display lower fracture strains and earlier onset of intergranular cracking.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to high-entropy alloys with comparable compositions and microstructures (e.g., precipitation-strengthened HEAs processed by SLM) under service conditions where deformation temperatures approach 650°C; grain sizes and precipitate distributions must also be within the ranges studied in the supporting literature.
generation.uncertainty: Variability in alloy composition, the influence of concurrent nano-precipitation, and processing-induced residual stresses may confound the sole effect of grain boundary morphology on toughness retention.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical high-entropy alloy samples. Process one set with a controlled slower cooling rate after solution treatment to induce serrated grain boundaries and the other set with a standard fast cooling to produce straight boundaries. Characterize the grain boundary morphology by high-resolution electron microscopy. Subject both sets to tensile and creep tests at 650°C to measure fracture strain and creep rupture life.
measurements: Grain boundary morphology (serration vs. straight) via TEM/SEM
Fractography to assess crack initiation sites
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the slow-cooled samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in fracture strain and creep rupture life compared to fast-cooled samples, or if the expected serrated grain boundary morphology is not observed, then the hypothesis that grain boundary morphology governs toughness retention via strain redistribution is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The formation of nano-sized Hf2Fe precipitates at grain boundaries through Fe micro-alloying enhances the strength of Ti-Zr-Hf-Nb-Ta multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs), but this improvement comes at the cost of reduced ductility. Aging at 500 °C for just 30 min resulted in a marked reduction in elongation, from 17.5% to 7.5%. This decline is attributed to lattice mismatch between the precipitates and the matrix, as well as increased stacking stress at the grain boundaries. By adjusting the Fe composition and heat treatment parameters, the quantity of Hf2Fe at the grain boundaries of (TiZrHfNbTa)100−xFex alloy was effectively controlled, achieving a balanced combination of strength of 1037 MPa and elongation of 14%. Furthermore, this method enabled ductility modulation over a wide range, with elongation varying from 2.65% to 19% while maintaining alloy strength between 955 and 1081 MPa, providing valuable insights for tailoring these alloys to diverse application requirements. In this work, the size and distribution of the nano-precipitated Hf2Fe at the grain boundaries of the HF alloys were tailored by fine-tuning the alloy composition and modifying heat treatment parameters. Six alloys with varying Fe composition and heat treatments were prepared, with detailed characterization of precipitate distribution and mechanical property testing. Additionally, the thermodynamics of the alloy system were investigated via CAPHAD by using TCHEA6, TCTI4, and TCNI12 databases in Thermo-Calc. According to the results and discussions, the following conclusions were obtained: The size and distribution of nano-sized precipitates at the grain boundaries are sensitive to both alloy composition and heat treatment parameters and have a critical impact on the mechanical properties of MPEAs. By slightly adjusting the alloy composition (0.15 at.%) and varying the heat treatment parameters, a series of alloys with a wide range of elongation from 2.65% to 19% were developed, while maintaining alloy strengths between 955 and 1081 MPa, providing design flexibility for diverse applications. cited_evidence.text: Although the ductility of the dual-phase HEA is lower than the single-phase HEA at the testing temperature below 500°C, the ductility of the dual-phase HEA is greater than the single-phase HEA at 600° and 700°C. No intergranular embrittlement is observed. Figure 5 (B and C) shows the lateral surface in the vicinity of the fracture after tensile tests at 500° and 700°C, respectively. Figure 5 (D and E) exhibits typical ductile dimples on fracture surfaces after tensile tests at 500° and 700°C, respectively. In contrast to single-phase samples (Fig. 3D), the dual-phase sample has very few cracks near the lateral fracture surface. This suggests that the GB segregation engineering strategy via preexisting Cr-rich precipitates is effective to evade ductility loss at intermediate temperatures in HEAs. This is because the embrittling elements—such as Cr, Mn, or Ni—can be absorbed by preexisting embrittling element–enriched precipitates at GBs, which only leads to the growth of precipitates rather than GB embrittlement. While strength and ductility are the global mechanical properties controlled by their bulk responses, fracture toughness originates from the resistance to crack initiation and propagation that is more closely related to the local microstructure and evolution. Therefore, the near-tip mechanisms revealed in this work, including the crystalline-to-amorphous phase transformation and formation of amorphous nanobridges, could be generally applicable to the toughening of other UFG HEAs. In conclusion, we have found the deformation-induced crystalline-to-amorphous phase transformation in the UFG Cantor alloy. The structural evolution exhibits a sequence of formation of the crystalline, lamellar, spotted, and amorphous patterns in TEM images that arise from different proportions and organizations of the crystalline and amorphous structures. The crack-tip high stresses, high lattice and grain boundary resistances to dislocation slip, and resulting accumulation of high-density dislocations are essential to the observed solid-state amorphization, thereby dissipating energy and resisting crack propagation. ABSTRACTIn this study, tensile and creep deformation of a high-entropy alloy processed by selective laser melting (SLM) has been investigated; hot ductility drop was identified at first, and the loss of ductility at elevated temperature was associated with intergranular fracture. By modifying the grain boundary morphology from straight to serration, the hot ductility drop issue has been resolved successfully. The serrated grain boundary could be achieved by reducing the cooling rate of solution heat treatment, which allowed the coarsening of L12 structured γ′ precipitates to interfere with mobile grain boundaries, resulting in undulation of the grain boundary morphology. Tensile and creep tests at 650°C were conducted, and serrated grain boundary could render a significant increase in tensile fracture strain and creep rupture life by a factor of 3.5 and 400, respectively. Detailed microstructure analysis has indicated that serrated grain boundary could distribute strains more evenly than that of straight morphology. papers.title: Investigation of the Micromechanical Behavior of a Ti68Nb7Ta3Zr4Mo18 (at.%) High-Entropy Alloy.
papers.approach: Molecular dynamics simulations under tensile conditions at various temperatures and strain rates
papers.findings: Observed a phase transformation from BCC to FCC, with grain boundary slip dominating at high temperatures and dislocation slip at low temperatures. Also noted an inverse Hall–Petch effect when grain size is very small.
papers.mechanism: Temperature and strain rate dictate which deformation pathway (grain boundary vs. dislocation slip) is activated and thereby influence the overall mechanical response, which can indirectly affect toughness retention by altering microstructural evolution.

papers.title: Ductility Control via Nano-Precipitation at Grain Boundaries in Ti-Zr-Hf-Nb-Ta Multi-Principal Element Alloys.
papers.system: Ti-Zr-Hf-Nb-Ta multi-principal element alloys with controlled Fe micro-alloying
papers.approach: Tailoring nano-precipitation (Hf2Fe) at grain boundaries via composition adjustments and heat treatment parameters; CALPHAD thermodynamic modeling was also used.
papers.findings: Demonstrated that nano-precipitates at GBs can enhance strength while reducing ductility if excessive; careful tuning allowed a balance between strength and ductility. Variations in precipitate distribution correlate with changes in mechanical performance.
papers.mechanism: Precipitate size and distribution influence lattice mismatch and stacking stress at grain boundaries, affecting dislocation motion and grain boundary cohesion—modes that critically govern toughness and its retention.

papers.title: Deformation-induced crystalline-to-amorphous phase transformation in a CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy.
papers.system: CrMnFeCoNi (Cantor) high-entropy alloy in ultrafine-grained and coarse-grained forms
papers.approach: In situ TEM straining experiments complemented with molecular dynamics simulations
papers.findings: Observed a deformation-induced crystalline-to-amorphous transformation at crack tips in UFG samples and formation of amorphous nanobridges that can delay crack propagation.
papers.mechanism: Local structural breakdown near crack tips leads to amorphization; the formation of nanoscale amorphous bridges dissipates energy and enhances toughness by impeding crack growth.

papers.title: Mitigating Strain Localization via Stabilized Phase Boundaries for Strengthening Multi-Principal Element Alloys.
papers.system: Multi-principal element alloys with enamel-inspired nanostructured BCC and FCC phases
papers.approach: Integrated macro/micro in situ mechanical tests, MD simulations, and DFT calculations to analyze the effect of stabilized phase boundaries
papers.findings: Establishes that engineered phase boundaries can provide additional plasticity space by facilitating dislocation transfer across phases, mitigating strain localization and delaying crack initiation.
papers.mechanism: Stabilized BCC/FCC phase boundaries act as zones for continuous dislocation transfer, ensuring distributed plasticity and reducing localized hardening that might otherwise lead to premature failure.

papers.title: Effect of serrated grain boundary on tensile and creep properties of a precipitation strengthened high entropy alloy.
papers.system: Precipitation-strengthened HEA processed by selective laser melting (SLM)
papers.approach: Modification of grain boundary morphology from straight to serrated via controlled cooling rates during solution heat treatment
papers.findings: Serrated grain boundaries increased tensile fracture strain and significantly improved creep rupture life by even factors of 3.5 to 400, attributed to redistributed strain fields.
papers.mechanism: Serration of grain boundaries, induced by the coarsening of L12 structured precipitates, reduces local strain concentration and improves resistance to intergranular cracking, thereby retaining toughness at elevated temperatures.

papers.title: Grain boundary decohesion by nanoclustering Ni and Cr separately in CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloys.
papers.approach: Atom probe tomography, TEM and SEM analyses to study nanoclustering at grain boundaries along with a GB segregation engineering strategy
papers.findings: Found that separate nanoclustering of principal elements (Ni, Cr, Mn) at grain boundaries decreases GB cohesion and leads to ductility loss at intermediate temperatures; additionally, incorporating preexisting Cr-rich precipitates can shift segregation away from GBs.
papers.mechanism: Fast segregation of embrittling elements into grain boundaries causes intergranular cracking; redirecting these elements via engineered precipitates can retain toughness by maintaining GB cohesion.

papers.title: Rejuvenation as the origin of planar defects in the CrCoNi medium entropy alloy.
papers.approach: In situ nanomechanical testing combined with energy-filtered 4D-STEM and MD simulations
papers.findings: Observed reversible stacking faults and twin boundaries becoming irreversible upon cyclic loading; linked these changes to local breakdown of SRO leading to a 'rejuvenated' state.
papers.mechanism: Rejuvenation via local SRO breakdown increases free energy locally, creating softer defect-rich planes that contribute to improved damage tolerance by altering crack propagation paths.

papers.title: Superhard bulk high-entropy carbides with enhanced toughness via metastable in-situ particles.
papers.approach: Sintering under varied pressures with XRD and microscopic analyses to monitor the phase state of ZrO2 particles
papers.findings: Higher sintering pressures promote retention of metastable tetragonal ZrO2 particles that transform martensitically under stress to the monoclinic form, resulting in crack deflection and improved fracture toughness.
papers.mechanism: Martensitic transformation of in situ ZrO2 particles contributes to energy absorption, while the transformation-induced crack deflection and bridging enhance the overall toughness of the carbide system.

established: The retention or loss of toughness in high-entropy alloys is closely tied to microstructural evolution during deformation, including phase transformations, grain boundary characteristics, and defect-mediated mechanisms.
Multiple deformation mechanisms (dislocation slip, twinning, phase transformation, and even amorphization) can synergistically contribute to damage tolerance and toughness.
Grain boundary segregation, nano-precipitation, and phase boundary stability are critical factors that influence both ductility and toughness in HEAs.

approaches_tried.approach: Tailoring nano-precipitation at grain boundaries via compositional adjustment and heat treatment (e.g., inducing Hf2Fe precipitates).
approaches_tried.outcome: Achieved a balance between strength and ductility over a wide range, but excessive precipitation can reduce ductility by increasing GB stress.

approaches_tried.approach: Engineering grain boundary morphology (serration) by modifying cooling rates in heat treatments.
approaches_tried.outcome: Significantly increased tensile fracture strain and improved creep life by reducing local strain concentrations at GBs.

approaches_tried.approach: Stabilizing phase boundaries in multi-principal element alloys to promote continuous dislocation transfer and mitigate strain localization.
approaches_tried.outcome: Enhanced strength and toughness through a synergy of traditional toughening mechanisms such as crack deflection, bridging, and blocking.

approaches_tried.approach: GB segregation engineering by redirecting embrittling element segregation into preexisting Cr-rich precipitates.
approaches_tried.outcome: Mitigated ductility loss at intermediate temperatures by preserving grain boundary cohesion.

mechanisms: Deformation-induced crystalline-to-amorphous phase transformation and formation of amorphous nanobridges.
Nano-precipitation at grain boundaries altering local stress states and controlling dislocation motion.
Stabilized phase boundaries (e.g., between BCC and FCC phases) providing extended plasticity and mitigating strain localization.
Grain boundary segregation (nanoclustering of Ni, Cr, Mn) leading to reduced cohesion and embrittlement.
Martensitic transformation of metastable precipitates (e.g., t-ZrO2 to m-ZrO2) under load that absorbs energy.
Local chemical ordering (or its breakdown) influencing dislocation pathways and defect mobility.
disagreements: Some studies emphasize amorphization and nanobridge formation as the primary toughening mechanism, while others focus on grain boundary segregation or phase boundary stabilization, reflecting different responses in varied HEA systems.

The role of nano-precipitates can be both beneficial and detrimental to toughness depending on their size, distribution, and the induced lattice mismatch, with some reports showing improved toughness and others noting ductility loss.
open_questions: What is the dominant mechanism governing toughness retention versus loss under controlled variations of temperature and strain rate in HEAs?

How do controlled compositional changes (e.g., slight alloying adjustments) interact with microstructural features (such as GB segregation and phase stability) to influence the transition in toughness?
Within which boundaries (thermal, strain rate, grain size) do these mechanisms reliably predict toughness, and how do they interplay?
Can direct experimental measurements correlate the onset of amorphization, phase transformation, or GB decohesion with quantifiable changes in fracture toughness?
opportunities: Design experiments that implement a controlled alteration—such as varying the heat-treatment cooling rate or minor alloying additions—to directly modulate grain boundary morphology or nano-precipitate distribution, with the aim to test the impact on toughness retention.
Combine phase boundary engineering with GB segregation control to synergistically enhance plasticity while reducing localized stress concentrations.
Develop in situ mechanical testing protocols at varying temperatures and strain rates to pinpoint the boundaries where mechanisms such as amorphization or hindered dislocation motion become dominant.

Utilize advanced characterization techniques (e.g., in situ TEM, 4D-STEM) in conjunction with atomistic simulations to directly observe the transition of microstructural features that correlate with toughness retention or loss, enabling falsification of competing mechanistic hypotheses.

directions.direction: Grain boundary morphology engineering by varying the solution treatment cooling rate to induce serrated versus straight grain boundaries.
directions.assessment: This direction directly affects the local strain distribution and crack‐initiation behavior via grain boundary morphology. It is strongly supported by evidence showing that serrated boundaries lead to improved tensile fracture strain and creep life (PMC9848264) and that grain boundary decohesion is correlated with ductility loss (PMC6897545). It is experimentally feasible and informative.

directions.direction: Nano‐precipitation tuning at grain boundaries by small alloying additions (e.g., Fe adjustments) and controlled aging, to balance strengthening and ductility.
directions.assessment: This approach addresses toughness retention by regulating precipitate size/distribution that affects lattice mismatch and stress concentration at grain boundaries (PMC11989734). It is well supported by thermodynamic modeling, but excessive precipitation may paradoxically reduce toughness if overdone.

directions.direction: Grain boundary segregation engineering through preexisting Cr‐rich secondary phases that absorb embrittling elements to avoid decohesion.
directions.assessment: This strategy directly targets the retention of ductility by modifying the chemical state of grain boundaries per evidence from PMC6897545. Although promising, it may be sensitive to composition and temperature boundaries.

directions.direction: Inducing in situ deformation‐induced phase transformation (e.g., crystalline‐to-amorphous conversion) near crack tips to create nanobridges.
directions.assessment: This mechanism, observed by in situ TEM (PMC8011962), explains how local amorphization can dissipate energy. However, controlling and quantifying such transformations under engineering conditions is challenging.

directions.direction: Stabilized phase boundary engineering to promote continuous dislocation transfer across coexisting BCC/FCC phases, mitigating localized hardening.
directions.assessment: This direction (supported by PMC12061292) links microstructural phase boundary stability to distributed plasticity and toughness. It is promising though it requires precise control over multiphase microstructures.

choice.direction: Grain boundary morphology engineering via controlled cooling rates to induce serrated boundaries.
choice.why: This approach most directly addresses the governing behavior of toughness retention by mitigating local strain concentrations at grain boundaries. It is strongly supported by experimental evidence (PMC9848264 and PMC6897545) and is technically feasible, offering clear, measurable changes in microstructure and mechanical response.
